description: Spain puts its own conquests on trial: Sepúlveda's natural-slavery argument against Las Casas's eyewitness testimony. No verdict — but the question survived.
essential_question: Could the conquest of the Americas be morally justified?

key_terms.definition: The 1550-51 council debate at Valladolid, Spain, over whether Spain's conquest of the Americas was just.
Spanish theologian who argued from Aristotle that Indigenous peoples were natural slaves and conquest was a just war.
Dominican friar whose fifty years in the Indies grounded his eyewitness case that Indigenous peoples were rational and Spanish cruelty was the true barbarism.
Sepúlveda's Aristotelian claim that some peoples are born to be ruled.
The idea first articulated at Valladolid that conquest itself can be judged by universal moral law.

learning_objectives: Summarize Sepúlveda's argument from natural slavery and its Aristotelian roots.
Explain Las Casas's defense of Indigenous peoples, including his tragic early irony.
Evaluate why the debate changed little on the ground but mattered for the history of rights.

narration.text: [solemn]In [date:1550], the most powerful empire on earth did something no Christian empire had ever done. [beat] Spain put its own conquests on trial. In Valladolid, a council of theologians and lawyers met to answer a single question: was the conquest of the Americas just, or was it a crime?

narration.text: For the conquest: Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda. Scholar. Logician. He had never set foot in the Americas. Never seen a single person he was about to describe. [VOICE:sepulveda][fierce] Aristotle settled this two thousand years ago. Some peoples are slaves by nature: born to be ruled, unfit to govern themselves. Their idolatry, their human sacrifices: these offend nature itself. A war that ends such practices is not cruelty.

narration.text: [solemn]So the debate changed nothing. And everything. Before Valladolid, no empire had formally asked whether winning a war could still make it wrong. Las Casas wrote the question down. The same man who once proposed African slavery to spare the Indians, then spent his life regretting it. The empire is gone. But the idea survived: conquest itself could be judged by [slow]universal moral law[/slow], the language of natural rights and human dignity. [pause:2]

scenes.production_notes: ASSET PENDING: lascasas-portrait-1791.webp (archival PD, to source). Slow push-in ending on the quill. Quill-scratch foley under the push-in. Cello drone returns in the final edit.

narration.text: [solemn]Here is the hardest part of his story. Years before Valladolid, Las Casas himself had proposed bringing enslaved Africans to the Indies, hoping to spare Indigenous workers. [beat] He spent the rest of his life regretting it. In his own history of the Indies, he wrote that he regretted the advice bitterly, and blamed himself for not seeing what it would become. [pause:1] The man who defended one people had helped condemn another. That is why his defense matters: it was not written by a saint. [emphasis]It was written by a man who knew exactly what guilt felt like.[/emphasis]
Every time we ask it about a war today, we're still sitting in [emphasis]that room[/emphasis].
